story_text.value:
Inspired by Karpathy's HackerTube, I wondered what was buried in "What are you working on?" thread comments. I wanted to see what changed, and who was still at it years later. So, I built this site to answer some of those questions.

A couple of things you can do: type in your idea and see who already tried it, look up your username and see what you were working on in 2020, see who’s been working on the same thing for a decade, or what founders posted before they had a company.

I built it using Claude Code. Claude Sonnet read all 20,982 top-level replies and pulled out a name, description, topic and how AI was involved. One finding is that AI went from 1% of answers in 2009–11 to 33% this year.

A few limits of the result: labels are model output, and I only spot-checked them. The HN thread only went monthly in 2024, so early years are thin. If I’ve mislabeled your project, or you’d rather not be included, please tell me.

If you’ve been posting here for years, I’d love to hear what happened to those projects.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Leon. I built Thrum which runs the coding agents you already use and gives them functionality to work as a team.

It started as an open source project late last year but then in May I went crazy and added a ton of features. I was using it every day to build itself and to do everything else I needed to do with agents. As I found limitations in what agents can do, I added features to the product.

The basic features were all there in a month or so and then I wrapped it all in the GUI. By this time the agents had sent over 200,000 messages and the whole thing fell over and I then had to spend 3 weeks fixing all of the cludge the agents had built and optimizing everyting. That got the performance to less then 1 second for any command and now the database I use has over 700,000 messages and the performance is still great.

Its full cloud infrastructure for your agents but is not cloud based. It connects over git, LAN, Tailscale, and soon SSH. The only data I see is the licensing part. I built it to run fully local so you choose where to spend your tokens.

It does everything I need to do any of the projects I work on so I just need to talk to one coordinator and they handle everything. I also created a steward ( like the steward on a ship ) and they watch all of my coordinators and important agenst like brainstormers and act as my steward to keep me up to date and I can tell it what to respond. It bugs me on telegram if I ignore it :)

The story: https://thrum.team/blog/launching-thrum-pro.html Give it a try-for free here: https://thrum.team Happy to answer any questions you have here.

Leon

story_text.value: Letting coding agents (such as Claude Code) work autonomously on repos on a daily-basis, brings a high level of uncertainty. For those who won't let the agent decide alone whether it can create/modify or delete any folder on their repos; I wanted to be able to trace actions performed and being able to let the agent continue his work autonomously, or ask him to request a human approval according to some criteria defined. After investigations, the cleanest way to do it was according to me to develop a deterministic control layer between the LLM and the work of the agent that would track and catch potential non-respect of pre-defined rules. How? by first setting up approval rules (Pass/requires approval/refused) before the work of the agent, and afterwards controlling cryptographic SHA 256 verifications, etc. This allows to compare the before-after work of the agent. I have put in my public GitHub repo a demo that you can launch easily and observe different scenarios behaviors like applied authorized modification, protected file waiting for Human approval, or outside perimeter authorization modification refused. The demo is offline, does not involve the official runtime, in native node.js and without dependencies. It should still allow you to understand the core principles. I would like to know: how do you implement and handle safety boundaries? Especially if you let agents work on critical data/sensitive codebases? With which guardrails?

story_text.value:
There is some recent discourse about what a "better" interface for humans managing agents looks like. Email/inboxes have come up, and it's reinforcing the premise of thing i've been building. e.g.

  - https://x.com/brian_armstrong/status/2119112609223827547
  - https://x.com/rough__sea/status/2119288646671155217?a=KRzp4CnuV6SijzvCTUw&s=20
This isn't 'another ADE', this is a side-car type of experience and it integrates nearly a year of work around annotating markdown, html, other artifacts since I requested the original Claude Code Hooks feature for better human-control integration.

The email inbox model is intuitive, but so could be "forums", slack-like, or other surfaces feel right.

I do not believe we will be working in coding sessions (full transcripts) much longer. I've been hitting flow-state on top of a better surface layer to make decisions and annotate artifacts, view variations, review code, etc all feedback going back to the agents

MIT/Apache2.0:

https://github.com/backnotprop/plannotator

story_text.value:
I built this because it was useful for me when building evals/benchmarks, and I decided to put it up for free for others. The goal was quite simple, make it easy to use a lead claude code / codex session in a panel on the side, while allowing every cell to also be a terminal session running claude/codex, and make it possible to continue a session in an actual terminal window if I needed to. They can all talk to each other using cells on the grid, named cells, or the MCP server that effectively glues the app together. I also found it useful for managing context within related but disparate sessions.

My real benchmark runs with recalc are internal to my startup, so to demonstrate some of the functionality I built a small FDA Bench with the tool (obtain and put together dossier's of FDA submissions, and see if a harnessed Claude could have accurately predicted pass/fail): https://github.com/sshah03/recalc#a-model-benchmark

It is still very much a work in progress, but given the versatility of spreadsheet apps, wanted to see how others see themselves using it and what doesn't exist that would be useful to them. Currently runs locally on macs, linux as well but that's less tested, and Windows hasn't been tested at all so that'll come in the future.

story_text.value:
Loop is a mobile-first companion workspace for the coding harnesses you already run. It aggregates results from your harnesses into a continuous feed that is easy to navigate and organize from your phone. I spent several months holding my newborn in one hand and trying to talk to agents one-handed on my phone. Every mobile UI is still based around chat, and it doesn’t scale on mobile, let alone one-handed!

So I built Loop: a feed of the work your coding agents do. It’s built around agent results, not chats. You can scroll your history, get notified, save outputs, search and return to conversations later. The goal is to make interacting with agents via your phone feel familiar and intuitive based on the mobile UX we’ve all come to expect.

Loop runs on your own computer — no account, no server, no app store — and pairs with your phone with one QR scan. It wraps the agents you already use (Codex, Claude Code, Pi, OpenCode, Antigravity, Muse Code, Grok Build, or any ACP agent), each keeping its own context, tools, sign-in and billing — local models through Pi or OpenCode work too.

Apache-2.0, TypeScript, SQLite. I'd love feedback from anyone else who builds from a phone.
